_about: Triage-as-code. Every number the risk engine uses lives here, not in the code. Change a weight, re-run, see the queue re-order.

business_hours._note: workdays are Python weekday() values: 0 = Monday .. 6 = Sunday.

malicious.reason: indicator is known-bad in threat intelligence

unknown.reason: indicator has no reputation data either way

internal.reason: indicator is a known internal asset, not an external destination

outside_business_hours.reason: activity occurred outside configured business hours

weekend.reason: activity occurred on a non-working day

privileged_account.reason: the acting account matches a privileged-account pattern

service_account.reason: a service account ran interactive-looking commands

external_destination.reason: the command line references a routable external address

metadata_endpoint.reason: the activity reaches the link-local instance metadata service, the usual route from a foothold on a cloud host to that host's credentials

external_origin.reason: the session originated from a routable external address rather than the console of the affected host - someone drove this from outside the network

internal_origin.reason: the session originated from another host on the internal network, which is the shape of lateral movement rather than local use

kill_chain_progression.reason: this account's alerts span multiple consecutive ATT&CK tactics, suggesting a progressing intrusion rather than an isolated event

repeat_rule.reason: the same detection fired repeatedly for this account

alert_burst.reason: many alerts for this account landed inside a short window

shared_origin.reason: one origin address touched several different accounts in a short window - the signature of password spraying, credential stuffing, or one stolen credential being reused across the network. Grouping alerts by account cannot see this: each account shows only a single unremarkable alert

_default: Confirm the parent process chain or the session context, whichever the telemetry carries.
Check whether a change ticket or deployment window explains this activity.
Record the verdict on the alert so the rule can be tuned.
Credential Access: Establish which credentials are actually implicated: a dumped secret store, or accounts targeted by repeated authentication attempts.
If a credential store or memory dump is involved, treat every credential used on this host as exposed and force a password reset for the affected account and any cached domain accounts.
If the evidence is failed authentication, check lockout policy and look for any attempt from the same origin that succeeded.
Pull the authentication trail for the affected accounts and the originating address across the alert window.
Command and Control: Block the external indicator at the egress proxy / firewall.
Pull full network flow for this host over the alert window.
Check whether other hosts contacted the same indicator.
Persistence: Enumerate autoruns, scheduled tasks and services created in the alert window.
Preserve the persistence artifact before removing it.
Verify the referenced binary's signature and hash.
Defense Evasion: Verify endpoint protection is still enabled and reporting.
Review any exclusion paths that were added and remove unapproved ones.
Assume telemetry gaps for the period after the tampering.
Initial Access: Retrieve the delivery artifact (attachment / link) and the mail headers.
Search the mail gateway for the same sender or lure across other recipients.
Confirm whether the user interacted with the content.
Lateral Movement: Identify the origin host and treat it as compromised until proven otherwise.
Pull the authentication trail: which accounts authenticated from that origin, and to what.
Check whether the credential used here was exposed by an earlier alert on the origin host.
Map what the destination host gives access to before deciding on containment.
Discovery: Correlate with the account's normal behaviour before escalating.
Discovery alone is weak evidence; look for what came before and after it.
Execution: Decode and read the actual command before judging intent.
Determine whether the interpreter run is user-initiated or spawned by another process.
Privilege Escalation: Establish which token or integrity level the process gained, and from what parent.
Check whether the account is expected to hold local administrator or elevation rights on this host.
Look at what the elevated context was used for immediately afterwards.
Collection: Identify what was staged, and where the archive or copy was written.
Determine the sensitivity of the data touched before deciding on escalation.
Watch for an outbound transfer following the staging.
Exfiltration: Quantify what left: bytes, destination and duration, from network flow.
Identify the data set involved and notify the data owner, and legal/privacy if it is regulated.
Block the destination at the egress point and check other hosts for the same destination.
Impact: Verify backup integrity, and that backups are offline or immutable, before anything else.
Establish blast radius: which hosts, shares and accounts are affected.
Make an explicit containment decision (host isolation, account disable) and record who authorised it.
Preserve a sample of the affected files and any ransom note before remediation.
